name: Rasm
baseline: SjasmPlus (Z80 cross-assembler). The README only says 'the best alternatives' and names no competitor; SjasmPlus is named in a CPCWiki snippet that could not be opened.
workload: Assembling Z80 assembly source (Amstrad CPC demo-scale projects, e.g. a 512K cartridge of about 350,000 words); no benchmark input is published in the repo.
claimed_speedup: README: 'peak performance around 100 millions instructions per second', 'tens of millions instructions per second on a modern CPU', 'way faster than the best alternatives' (no ratio or competitor on the README page).
tradeoffs: Z80 family only (Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and similar); not a replacement for GNU as, NASM or MASM. README recommends the mimalloc build ('make superfastmi') on Linux for extra speed.
caveats: First-party claim without a published benchmark input, command line or competitor table (no benchmark directory in the top-level listing). Ratios were seen only in WebSearch snippets of pages that could not be opened (cpcwiki.eu and depot.haiku-os.org both failed to resolve): CPCWiki about 1 million lines in 0.03 s and '100x faster than SjasmPlus'; Haiku depot '30 times faster than his best challenger'; the multiplier differs between sources. The sjasmplus README (opened) separately claims '1 million lines by 2-3 seconds', which is consistent with a large ratio but was measured by a different author on unknown machines. Baseline is not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/z80-assembler (sjasmplus README names Rasm), then WebSearch 'Z80 assembler speed comparison rasm sjasmplus vasm pasmo ... benchmark'; opened github.com/EdouardBERGE/rasm and its commits page

name: KeplerAs and SGEMM assembly (PPoPP 2017 artifact)
language: SASS assembly kernels plus an assembler (implementation language not confirmed; README says KeplerAs is based on MaxAs)
baseline: NVIDIA cuBLAS 7.0 SGEMM (and cuDNN v4.0 for the convolution kernel), i.e. NVIDIA's library kernels built by NVIDIA's own toolchain
workload: Single-precision GEMM on an NVIDIA Tesla K20m, square matrices 384 to 12288 (step 384) and rectangular shapes, plus a convolution kernel on the same GPU (batch size 128).
claimed_speedup: Paper (sgemm.pdf in the repo): at 12288 x 12288 the hand-assembled SGEMM reaches 3.1 Tflop/s (88% of peak) versus cuBLAS 7.0 at 2.7 Tflop/s (76%), a 1.15x speedup; convolution kernel 39%, 46% and 62% faster than cuDNN v4.0 for three CNN configurations.
compiler_and_flags: cuBLAS from CUDA 7.0 as the baseline; the optimized kernels are written directly in SASS and assembled with KeplerAs, so no nvcc flags apply. Compiler flags for any host harness are not stated on the pages opened.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla K20m (host CPU model not stated on the pages opened)
tradeoffs: Kepler-only SASS (the ISA encoding was cracked for Kepler and differs from Maxwell); kernels and the assembler do not carry over to newer GPUs. The same research line produced MaxAs (Maxwell/Pascal) and TuringAs (Volta/Turing/Ampere).
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (PPoPP 2017, title in the repo README 'Understanding the GPU Microarchitecture to Achieve Bare-Metal Performance Tuning') but the repo shows no license and the opened README and directory pages give no run scripts or benchmark harness, so the numbers are not reproducible from what was opened (hence B, not A). cuBLAS 7.0 is from 2015 and has since been replaced. The comparison is hand-written assembly against a vendor library, not an assembler-versus-assembler speed test; baseline is not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: daadaada/turingas README 'Related projects' links KeplerAs to this artifact repo; opened github.com/PAA-NCIC/PPoPP2017_artifact and fetched sgemm.pdf from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: K2 (smartnic/superopt, BPF superoptimizing compiler)
language: C++ (inferred from main.cc and z3server.cc in the file listing; the Languages bar was empty)
baseline: clang-compiled BPF bytecode (best clang output; optimization level not confirmed from an opened page)
workload: Superoptimizing eBPF programs from Cilium, Facebook and the Linux kernel samples for program size, average packet-processing latency and throughput.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search summary of arXiv 2103.00022, not opened): 6-26% smaller code, 1.36%-55.03% lower average packet-processing latency and 0-4.75% higher throughput than the best clang-compiled program.
tradeoffs: BPF bytecode only; needs the z3 SMT solver (README install steps build main_ebpf.out against z3); the search runs offline at compile time, cost not seen.
caveats: Numbers come only from a WebSearch summary of the paper: arXiv, ar5iv and the K2 project site (k2.cs.rutgers.edu) were all unreachable. The repo README is install-only ('Todo: add more instructions soon') and carries no benchmark data. Baseline is clang BPF output, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. Paper-access retier lead: would likely become B if the PDF is read.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'K2 BPF superoptimizer smartnic superopt github clang -O3 fewer instructions lower latency'; opened github.com/smartnic/superopt and its commits page

name: TuringAs (SASS assembler for Volta, Turing and Ampere)
baseline: NVIDIA cuDNN 7.6.1 (Winograd convolution kernels that the PPoPP 2020 paper wrote with this assembler)
workload: Batched Winograd convolution on NVIDIA Volta/Turing GPUs (paper 'Optimizing Batched Winograd Convolution on GPUs', which the README asks users to cite).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search summary of the paper, PDF not opened): Winograd convolution reaches up to 93% of device peak and up to 2.65x speedup over cuDNN 7.6.1. The repo README has no numbers.
tradeoffs: SASS for SM70, SM75 and SM80 only; many instruction classes are marked TODO in the README (type conversion, LDSM, texture, surface, uniform datapath).
caveats: The speedup belongs to the paper's convolution kernels, not to this repo: the repo has only an assembler plus examples (bench/smem, copy_element), and the Winograd kernels were not found in the author's public repository list. The paper host (home.cse.ust.hk) did not resolve, so the numbers are snippet only. Baseline is cuDNN, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. Weak entry; keep as a paper-access retier lead.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/assembler page 2 listed CuAssembler; its sibling TuringAs found via WebSearch 'SASS assembler github hand-tuned SASS kernel outperforms cuBLAS ...'; opened github.com/daadaada/turingas, its commits page and examples directory

name: z88dk (Z80 development kit: C compilers, z80asm assembler and assembly libraries)
baseline: SDCC 4.6.0 (also HI-TECH C 3.09 and 7.80 and IAR Z80 V4.06A in the same tables)
workload: Z80 cycle counts and code size for Dhrystone 2.1, Whetstone 1.2, n-Body, Fasta, Pi, Sieve, Fannkuch and Binary-Trees compiled by each toolchain and run on the z88dk-ticks Z80 emulator (wall clock derived at 4 MHz).
claimed_speedup: From the wiki Benchmarks tables, cycles SDCC vs z88dk classic library: n-Body 4,361,393,645 vs 2,243,368,504 (1.94x fewer, derived from page data) and vs 860,188,405 with --math32 (5.07x, derived); Whetstone 1,850,296,726 vs 916,750,272 (2.02x, derived) and vs 360,608,050 with math32 (5.13x, derived); Fasta 414,019,207 vs 241,418,675 (1.71x, derived); Pi 7,218,092,827 vs 4,010,854,332 (1.80x, derived); Dhrystone 274,542,684 vs 242,442,688 (1.13x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Per-result settings listed in each benchmark readme; for n-Body, e.g. 'classic +test, -compiler=sdcc -SO3 --math32' with zsdcc 4.6.0 #16639 against SDCC 4.6.0 #16608; defines -DSTATIC, -DPRINTF, -DTIMER, -DCOMMAND. Only the n-body readme was opened.
hardware: z88dk-ticks Z80 emulator (cycle-exact count; wall time assumes a 4 MHz Z80), not a physical CPU
license: Clarified Artistic License (SPDX ClArtistic) 'unless otherwise stated in the appropriate file'
tradeoffs: Z80-family targets only; the speed comes from hand-written assembly libraries and a cheaper calling convention, with larger code in several rows (SDCC is smaller on Sieve, Fannkuch and Dhrystone sizes).
caveats: The win is not uniform: with the NEW library Binary-Trees takes 6,570,984,020 cycles against 193,466,493 for plain SDCC (about 34x slower; the wiki blames a realloc free-block search, issue #113), and HI-TECH C 7.80 is faster and smaller than all others on Fannkuch. Rows without a MATH32 label use pre-v2.5 float libraries and are not comparable to MATH32 rows. The baseline is a C compiler, not GNU as, NASM or MASM, and the z80asm assembler itself is not benchmarked, so category fit is weak. Per-benchmark flags beyond n-body not opened. Licence is not confirmed OSI-approved and individual files may differ.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/assembler page 2 (z88dk/z88dk, 1.1k stars); README 'Benchmarks' section points to the wiki and support/benchmarks
